title: Leading Learning : One essential lesson from Keir Starmer
author: Martin Skelton
summary: Using Keir Starmer's collapsing premiership as a springboard, Skelton argues that leaders fail when they manage competently but never articulate a direction. He restates his distinction between leadership as doing the right thing by building consensus and management as doing things right by securing consent. Borrowing Freud's idea of the narcissism of small differences, he says similar groups fight hardest over minor points, and he recalls the wasted hours he spent in such arguments in schools. His one essential lesson is that leaders must rise above these differences and keep naming the shared direction and the progress being made. He closes with reflective questions for school and classroom leaders about whether learning is the direction of travel.
points: Starmer is presented as a capable manager but not a viable leader because he could not state a clear direction and so could not build consensus.
The narcissism of small differences means closely aligned colleagues spend their energy on minor disagreements, hiding their shared purpose.
Leaders should name what people have in common and the progress they are making, accepting differences without letting them dominate.
Many schools and classrooms lack a big idea at all, and even when they have one, leaders often feed small-difference disputes.
quotes: One of the most important reasons why Starmer’s time in office has not caught fire and one of the reasons why so many of his own Members of Parliament and voters no longer want him to be Prime Minister is that he has been a competent manager but he isn’t a viable leader. Very few people want to follow him because he can’t articulate clearly a direction in which to go. As a consequence, he can’t build a consensus.
Leadership is not about getting involved in the weeds of things. That’s management’s job. Leadership is about staying above the fray and pointing in the right direction.

I can’t count the wasted hours of my life spent in arguing arcane points about curriculum, about teacher performance, about structures and systems, about shared agreements and more. All to no real avail.

When we get overwhelmed by the narcissism of small differences we replace consensus with separation. When we allow small differences to become the way we do things around here we make invisible any consensus or collective focus on the direction we are travelling.

As leaders, we have to rise above the narcissism of small differences. We have to do that because identifying a general direction in which to travel and communicating how we are doing is a more important leadership activity than arguing about each minor road along which we might travel.

Leadership articulates what we have in common, the progress we are collectively making and how much better we are getting, notwithstanding the differences we have. Leadership accepts the differences but doesn’t let them become the star, unless they really matter.
Do you think that your colleagues or your students have a real awareness that learning is the direction of travel? Do you think they feel collectively similar about how learning is getting better?
